'''''Carya ovata''''', the '''shagbark hickory''', is a common [[hickory]] native to eastern North America, with two [[Variety (botany)|varieties]]. The trees can grow to quite a large size but are unreliable in their fruit output. The nut is consumed by wildlife and historically by Native Americans, who also used the wood.

==Name==
The word ''hickory'' is an [[Apheresis (linguistics)|aphetic]] form from earlier ''pohickory'', short for even earlier ''pokahickory'', borrowed from the Virginia [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian]] word ''pawcohiccora'', hickory-nut meat or a [[Plant milk|nut milk]] drink made from it.<ref name="Hilton">[http://www.hiltonpond.org/ThisWeek030908.html Hilton Pond Center: Shaggybark Tree].  Retrieved 2013-08-10.</ref> Other names for this tree are Carolina Hickory, Scalybark Hickory, Upland Hickory, and Shellbark Hickory, with older [[Binomial nomenclature|binomial names]] of ''Carya ovata var. fraxinifolia'', ''Carya ovata var. nuttallii'', ''Carya ovata var. pubescens'', ''Hicoria alba'', ''Hicoria borealis'', and ''Hicoria ovata''.<ref>{{cite web
 |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=caov2
 |title=PLANT DATABASE: Carya ovata
 |date=2015-12-15
 |publisher=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center, The University of Texas at Austin
 |access-date=2020-03-09}}</ref>

== Description ==
It is a large, [[deciduous]] tree, growing well over {{convert|100|ft|m|0|abbr=on}} tall, and can live more than 350<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eastern OLDLIST: A database of maximum tree ages for Eastern North America |url=http://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/~adk/oldlisteast/#spp}}</ref> years. The tallest measured shagbark, located in Savage Gulf, Tennessee, is over {{convert|150|ft|m|0|abbr=on}} tall.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Trees |url=https://www.adventuresci.org/visit/arboretum/shagbark-hickory/ |access-date=2025-10-18 |website=Adventure Science Center |language=en-US}}</ref> Mature shagbarks are easy to recognize because, as their name implies, they have shaggy bark. This characteristic is, however, only found on mature trees; young specimens have smooth bark.

The [[leaves]] are {{convert|30|-|60|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long, [[pinnate]], with five (rarely three or seven) leaflets, the terminal three leaflets much larger than the basal pair. The shagbark hickory is [[monoecious]]. Staminate flowers are borne on long-stalked [[catkins]] at the tip of old wood or in the axils of the previous season's leaves. Pistillate flowers occur in short terminal spikes.<ref>Tirmenstein, D. A. 1991. "Carya ovata." In: ''Fire Effects Information System'' [Online]. U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station, Fire Sciences Laboratory (Producer).[http://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/tree/carova/all.html]. Retrieved 2013-08-10.</ref> The [[fruit]] is a [[drupe]] {{convert|2.5|to|4|cm|frac=4|abbr=on}} long, an edible [[nut (fruit)|nut]] with a hard, bony shell, contained in a thick, green four-sectioned husk which turns dark and splits off at maturity in the fall.<ref name="Hilton" /> The terminal buds on the shagbark hickory are large and covered with loose scales.<ref name="Barnes">{{cite book |last=Barnes |first=Burton V. |title=Michigan trees: a Guide to the Trees of the Great Lakes Region |last2=Wagner, Jr. |first2=Warren H. |publisher=University of Michigan Press |year=2004 |isbn=0-472-08921-8 |edition=Revised and updated |location=Ann Arbor |pages=272–273}}</ref>

''C. ovata'' begins producing seeds at about 10 years of age, but large quantities are not produced until 40 years and will continue for at least 100. Nut production is erratic, with good crops every 3 to 5 years, in between which few or none appear and the entire crop may be lost to animal predation.

== Taxonomy ==
The two varieties are:
*''Carya ovata'' var. ''ovata'' (northern shagbark hickory) has its largest leaflets over {{convert|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and nuts {{convert|3|-|4|cm|frac=8|abbr=on}} long.
*''Carya ovata'' var. ''australis'' (southern shagbark hickory or Carolina hickory) has its largest leaflets under {{convert|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} long and nuts {{convert|2|-|3|cm|frac=8|abbr=on}} long.

Some sources regard southern shagbark hickory as the separate species ''Carya carolinae-septentrionalis''.<ref>[http://www.cas.vanderbilt.edu/bioimages/species/caca38.htm Bioimages: ''Carya carolinae-septentrionalis''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060216085336/http://www.cas.vanderbilt.edu/bioimages/species/caca38.htm|date=2006-02-16}}. Retrieved 2013-08-10.</ref>

== Distribution ==
Shagbark hickory is found throughout most of the eastern United States, but it is largely absent from the [[Atlantic Plain|southeastern]] and [[Gulf Coastal Plain]]s and lower [[Mississippi Delta]] areas.<ref>{{Silvics |last=Graney |first=David L. |volume=2 |genus=Carya |species=ovata |access-date=2013-08-10}}</ref>  An isolated population grows in eastern Canada as far north as Lavant Township, Canadian zone 4b.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Lavant Shagbarks|url=http://johnsankey.ca/crf/lavant.html|publisher=Eastern Chapter Society of Ontario Nut Growers|access-date=2016-06-09|date=2010-01-26}}</ref>  Scattered locations of shagbark hickory occur in the [[Sierra Madre Oriental]] of eastern [[Mexico]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.floridata.com/ref/c/cary_ova.cfm |title=#836 Carya ovata |last=Christman |first=Steve |date=2003-11-09|website=Floridata.com |access-date=2012-09-30}}</ref>

Shagbark hickory was introduced in Europe in the 17th century. It can still be found in [[Central Europe]] as a non-native species.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wilgan|first1=Robin|last2=Leski|first2=Tomasz|last3=Kujawska|first3=Marta|last4=Karliński|first4=Leszek|last5=Janowski|first5=Daniel|last6=Rudawska|first6=Maria|date=2020-04-01|title=Ectomycorrhizal fungi of exotic Carya ovata in the context of surrounding native forests on Central European sites|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1754504818303143|journal=Fungal Ecology|language=en|volume=44|article-number=100908|doi=10.1016/j.funeco.2019.100908|s2cid=214538885|issn=1754-5048|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The native geographical range is one of the widest among Hickory species, although the species is less prevalent now due to selective harvesting for wood.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilgan |first1=Robin |last2=Leski |first2=Tomasz |last3=Kujawska |first3=Marta |last4=Karlinski |first4=Leszek |last5=Janowski |first5=Daniel |last6=Rudawska |first6=Maria |title=Ectomycorrhizal fungi of exotic Carya ovata in the context of surrounding native forests on Central European sites |journal=Fungal Ecology |date=4 February 2020 |volume=44}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
[[American red squirrel|Red squirrels]], [[Eastern gray squirrel|gray squirrels]], [[raccoon]]s, [[chipmunks]], and [[mice]] are consumers of hickory nuts.<ref name=":1">{{cite web |last=Beaulieu |first=David |title=Growing Shagbark Hickories, Harvesting Hickory Nuts |url=http://landscaping.about.com/od/fallfoliagetrees/a/hickory_trees_2.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130513092204/http://landscaping.about.com/od/fallfoliagetrees/a/hickory_trees_2.htm |archive-date=2013-05-13 |access-date=2013-08-10 |website=about.com}}</ref> Other consumers include  [[American black bear|black bears]], gray and red foxes, rabbits, and bird species such as mallards, wood ducks, bobwhites, and wild turkey.<ref>{{cite web |title=Shagbark Hickory Tree |url=http://www.cirrusimage.com/tree_shagbark_hickory.htm |access-date=2013-08-10 |website=cirrusimage.com |publisher=Red Planet Inc.}}</ref>

== Uses ==
[[File:Carya ovata Noyer blanc.jpg|thumb|left|''Carya ovata'' fruit]]
[[File:Carya ovata mature fruit.jpg|thumb|Mature fruit]]
[[File:Shagbark hickory spring leaf cluster.jpg|thumb|''Carya ovata'' spring leaf cluster]]
[[File:Phylloxera. Carya ovata. Leaf.jpg|thumb|''[[Phylloxera (genus)|Phylloxera]] caryaeglobuli'' galls on ''C. ovata'' leaves]]

The nuts are edible<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=243|oclc=244766414|orig-date=Originally published in 1982}}</ref> with an excellent flavor. They are unsuitable for commercial or orchard production due to the long time it takes for a tree to produce sizable crops and unpredictable output from year to year. The nuts can be used as a substitute for the [[pecan]]<ref name=":0" /> in colder climates and have nearly the same culinary function. The bark is also used to flavor a [[maple syrup|maple]]-style syrup.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bergo |first=Alan |date=2022-10-12 |title=Shagbark Hickory Syrup |url=https://foragerchef.com/hickory-syrup/ |access-date=2025-10-18 |website=Forager {{!}} Chef |language=en-US}}</ref>

Shagbark hickory nuts were an important staple of indigenous diet. Excavation of  an ancient (ca. 4350–4050 cal BP) site at Victor Mills in Columbia County, Georgia found hickory nuts, processing tools and other artifacts indicating large-scale processing and storage of nuts.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sassaman |first1=Kenneth E. |last2=Bartz |first2=Emily R. |date=3 April 2022 |title=Hickory nut storage and processing at the Victor Mills site (9CB138) and implications for Late Archaic land use in the middle Savannah River valley |journal=Southeastern Archaeology |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=79–97 |doi=10.1080/0734578X.2022.2033450}}</ref> [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] used the kernel milk to make corn cakes, [[kanuchi]] and [[hominy]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Grauke |first=LJ |title=Hickories: ''Carya ovata'' |url=http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/carya/species/ovata/ovata.htm |access-date=2013-08-10 |publisher=Texas A&M University, Department of Horticultural Science |archive-date=2011-12-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111202184601/http://aggie-horticulture.tamu.edu/carya/species/ovata/ovata.htm }}</ref><ref name="eastern" /> The nuts were a significant food source for the Algonquins.<ref name=":1" /> Shagbark hickory [[wood]] is used for [[smoking (food)|smoking]] [[meat]] and for making the [[bow (weapon)|bows]] of Native Americans of the northern area.  The lumber is heavy, hard, and tough, weighing 63 lb/ cu ft when air-dried,<ref>Collingwood, C.H., and Warren D. Brush. 1974. ''Knowing Your Trees''. Revised and edited by Devereux Butcher. Washington, District of Columbia: The American Forestry Association.  pp. 168–169.</ref> and has been employed for implements and tools that require strength.  These include axles, axe handles, ploughs, skis, and drum sticks.<ref>{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |title=Trees You Want to Know |publisher=Whitman Publishing Company |year=1934 |location=Racine, Wisconsin}}</ref>{{page needed|date=January 2024}}

== In culture ==
[[Andrew Jackson]], the seventh president of the United States, was popularly nicknamed Old Hickory, a play on the toughness of hickory wood.<ref name=eastern>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=353}}</ref> In 1830, he began planning the construction of his tomb at [[The Hermitage (Nashville, Tennessee)|The Hermitage]], his plantation in [[Tennessee]]. The grave site was surrounded by a variety of trees, including six shagbark hickories. They stood there for 168 years until a storm in 1998 demolished over 1,200 trees at the site. Work on replanting them remains an ongoing project. In modern times, shagbark hickory is rarely used as an ornamental due to its large size, slow growth, difficulty of transplanting (all Juglandaceae species have large taproots) and nut litter.

== Genetics ==
Shagbark hickory hybridizes with [[Carya illinoensis|pecan]], ''Carya illinoensis'', and shellbark hickory, ''C. laciniosa'' (''C. ''x'' dunbarii'' Sarg.). Shagbark hickory has 32 chromosomes. In general, species within the genus with the same chromosome number are able to cross. Numerous hybrids among the ''Carya'' species with 32 chromosomes (pecan, [[Carya cordiformis|bitternut]], [[Carya laciniosa|shellbark]], and shagbark) have been described, though most are unproductive or have other flaws.  A few [[hican]] varieties are commercially propagated.
